result: The manuscript establishes the identity and opposing functions of Dop1R1 and Dop2R as D1- and D2-like dopamine receptors in Drosophila, drawing parallels to mammalian dopamine receptor systems.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C11-C15 are well-supported by citations to prior work establishing the receptor identities, G-protein coupling, and opposing regulation of cAMP levels. These are established facts from the literature that provide necessary background context.

result: Dop1R1 and Dop2R show overlapping expression in Drosophila brain with co-expression in PAM neurons and Kenyon cells, but selective expression in other cell types including ring neurons and ensheathing glia.
evaluation: Claims C16-C17 cite prior RNA-seq and expression profiling work, while C28-C34 present new imaging data (Figure 1) showing expression patterns. The combination of prior work and new visualization data strongly supports the overlapping yet selective expression patterns.

result: The GFP11-tagged dopamine receptors retain functional integrity and do not perturb protein localization or function.
evaluation: Claims C35 and C76 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showing comparable memory scores between tagged and untagged receptors. This validates the tagging approach for subsequent localization studies.

result: Dop1R1 and Dop2R proteins are distributed throughout Kenyon cell membranes with enrichment in the lobes and sparse distribution in the calyx, with Dop2R showing more pronounced lobe enrichment than Dop1R1.
evaluation: Claims C37-C40 are supported by imaging data (Figure 3A-D) and quantitative localization index measurements showing statistically significant differences between receptors and between subcellular compartments. The consistency across experimental batches (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) strengthens the findings.

result: Both Dop1R1 and Dop2R are enriched at presynaptic and postsynaptic sites in Kenyon cells, with Dop2R showing greater presynaptic localization than Dop1R1.
evaluation: Claims C3-C5 and C41-C44 are supported by high-resolution Airyscan imaging (Figure 4B-C) showing receptor signals around Brp puncta (presynaptic) and adjacent to non-KC Brp clusters (postsynaptic). The quantitative comparison (Figures 3D, 7E) demonstrates differential enrichment between receptors.

result: Presynaptic localization of dopamine receptors is heterogeneous across release sites and independent of circuit context, as demonstrated in both Kenyon cells and giant neurons.
evaluation: Claims C45-C46 are supported by imaging showing not all Brp puncta associate with receptors (Figure 5A). Claims C49-C53 use giant neurons as an independent system, showing similar receptor-Brp associations (Figure 5B-C), supporting circuit-independent localization.

result: In MBON-γ1pedc>αβ neurons, both Dop1R1 and Dop2R are enriched in dendritic projections in the γ1 compartment and detected in presynaptic boutons.
evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by imaging data (Figure 6B-C) showing dendritic enrichment contrasting with sparse dendritic distribution in KCs, and presynaptic detection consistent with KC and giant neuron findings.

result: Both Dop1R1 and Dop2R localize to presynaptic terminals of PAM dopamine neurons, with Dop2R showing stronger presynaptic enrichment, suggesting dual feedback regulation as autoreceptors.
evaluation: Claims C59-C63 are supported by imaging data (Figure 7A-F) showing polarized PAM neurons with receptor localization to terminals and quantitative LI measurements. Claim C64 (and C6) infers autoreceptor function from localization, which is reasonable but requires functional validation.

result: Starvation induces bidirectional modulation of dopamine receptor expression in PAM neurons, with increased Dop1R1 and decreased or unchanged Dop2R, shifting the balance to enhance presynaptic dopamine signaling.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9 and C66 are supported by quantitative imaging data (Figure 8B-C) showing significant time-dependent changes with starvation. Claim C67 interprets these changes as shifting receptor balance, which is a reasonable inference from the data.

result: Starvation increases Dop2R but not Dop1R1 in PPL1 neurons, representing opposite changes from PAM neurons and suggesting bidirectional modulation of the dual autoreceptor system.
evaluation: Claims C10, C68-C69 are supported by imaging data (Figure 8D-F) showing differential receptor expression in PPL1 neurons and opposite starvation responses compared to PAM. Claim C70 synthesizes these findings into a bidirectional modulation model.

result: Starvation-induced changes in the dual autoreceptor system shift the balance to favor PAM output over PPL1, contributing to appetitive behavior expression, as demonstrated by impaired appetitive memory upon Dop2R knockdown in PPL1 neurons.
evaluation: Claims C71 cites prior work on PPL1 function. Claims C72-C74 propose a model linking receptor changes to behavior, supported by behavioral data (Figure 9C) showing impaired appetitive memory with Dop2R knockdown. Claims C96-C97 synthesize the overall model with supporting citations.

result: The CRISPR/Cas9-based split-GFP tagging approach enables flexible, sensitive detection of low-abundant endogenous proteins with negligible background.
evaluation: Claims C75 and C77 cite prior work on the advantages of CRISPR/Cas9 and split-GFP approaches. Claims C78-C79 describe technical advantages observed in this study, supported by the quality of imaging data throughout and specific reference to Figure 8D.

result: The differential spatial distribution of Dop1R1 and Dop2R may enhance sensitivity and precision of dopaminergic modulation through distinct responses to extrasynaptic versus synaptic dopamine.
evaluation: Claims C80-C81 cite prior work on volume transmission. Claims C82-C84 propose functional interpretations of the observed spatial distributions, but these are speculative hypotheses requiring experimental validation of receptor activation by extrasynaptic versus synaptic dopamine.

result: Presynaptic receptor localization suggests spatially confined cAMP nanodomains that regulate synaptic function and underlie associative memory in Kenyon cells.
evaluation: Claims C85-C87 cite prior work on cAMP nanodomains and memory mechanisms. Claim C88 connects presynaptic receptor localization to memory requirements, but this is an inference requiring direct demonstration of cAMP dynamics and their relationship to receptor localization.

result: The dual autoreceptor system likely fine-tunes dopamine release amplitude and kinetics, with Dop2R providing negative feedback and Dop1R1 potentially providing positive feedback for signal amplification.
evaluation: Claim C89 cites prior work on Dop2R negative regulation. Claims C90-C94 propose a model of dual feedback regulation based on localization patterns and expression differences, but functional validation of autoreceptor activity and effects on dopamine release is needed.

result: Background information on mushroom body circuit organization, dopamine neuron functions, and prior knowledge of receptor expression and regulation.
evaluation: These claims (C18-C27, C36, C47-C48, C57-C58, C65, C95) provide essential background context from prior literature, all supported by appropriate citations. They establish the foundation for interpreting the current findings.
